issues.description: The confidence scale is reported inconsistently within Experiment 1. The figure caption describes a 1–4 confidence scale, but the Procedure later states participants clicked one of two boxes, 1–2. This inconsistency makes it unclear how confidence was actually measured and what threshold defined 'high confidence,' directly affecting the main analyses that depend on high-confidence trials.
issues.quote:
Figure 1 ... Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty).
...
After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly analyzes only 'high confidence trials' but never clearly specifies, for each experiment, what confidence values counted as high confidence. Because the confidence scale itself is inconsistently reported and no thresholding rule is given, the central dependent variable cannot be reproduced or evaluated.
issues.quote:
For each memory delay ... the occurrence of illusory errors ... was calculated.
...
Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design ...
...
Figure 2 shows the illusory and other error rates in high confidence trials.

issues.description: Participants were excluded after data collection for having too few high-confidence critical trials in one or more design cells. This exclusion is based on the focal dependent variable and may systematically select participants who are more confident and/or more susceptible to the effect, biasing estimates and undermining generalizability. In Experiment 2, 92/290 participants (31.7%) were excluded; in Experiment 1, the arithmetic is also unclear. No sensitivity analyses including all participants are reported.
issues.quote:
Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) ...
...
Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) ...

issues.description: The rule requiring more than 10 high-confidence trials per cell appears arbitrary and is not justified, preregistered, or sensitivity-tested. Because critical-trial frequencies differ by target type and experiment, this threshold can materially change the sample retained and the estimated effects. This is a substantial researcher degree of freedom.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) ...

issues.description: Experiment 1 participant accounting is inconsistent. The manuscript states 45 started training, 5 were excluded based on training, leaving 40; later it states exclusion based on too few high-confidence critical trials resulted in inclusion of 23 participants and that '5 participants were excluded,' which does not reconcile with 40 initial post-training participants. Twelve participants are unaccounted for.
issues.quote:
45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants...
...
Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the text states that for non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was relevant and that non-illusory errors increased from short to long delay with BFincl = 190. However, Table 4 reports BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay and very strong evidence for Target Type (39110.895), the exact opposite pattern. This is a serious contradiction in the core results.
issues.quote:
For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42... ). Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) ...
...
Table 4 ... Memory Delay ... BFincl | 0.064
Target Type ... BFincl | 39110.895

issues.description: Experiment 4 Results refers to 'Figure 5' for Experiment 4 error rates, but the next figure is labeled Figure 6 and Figure 5 was already used for Experiment 3. This reflects poor internal consistency and raises concern about figure-result alignment.
issues.quote:
Results

Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.
...
Figure 6 Experiment 4. Error rates in trials where participants indicated high confidence in their response.

issues.subcategory: overclaim that delay increase rules out perceptual encoding
issues.description: The central inference that increasing error rates over time demonstrates memory illusions rather than perceptual/encoding errors is too strong. An initial weak, ambiguous, or partially misencoded percept could interact with retention interval, interference, decision noise, and response processes to produce more later errors without requiring that a veridical representation was first stored and then 'converted' into an illusion. Thus the design does not cleanly separate perceptual from memory-stage origins.
issues.quote:
If the frequency of reported illusions increases over time, then at least part of the illusions can be attributed to memory processing rather than perceptual encoding.
...
This effect must be due to processes ongoing in STM: Had these illusory memories been the result of changes in perception, they should have been present at the earlier probe as well.

issues.subcategory: causal claims from retention-interval manipulation without isolating response bias
issues.description: The manuscript interprets increased selection of real-letter counterparts over time as evidence that expectations reshape memory traces. But the task conflates memory, decision, and response bias. As uncertainty increases with delay, participants may increasingly choose the more familiar/expected option at decision time, without the underlying stored representation having changed. No model or control separates memory-trace distortion from decisional criterion shifts.
issues.quote:
Together, these experiments show that expectations can reshape perceptual representations over short time scales...
...
Over time illusions become more prevalent, indicating that correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter.

issues.subcategory: confidence does not validate false-memory phenomenology
issues.description: The manuscript equates high confidence errors with 'actual' illusory memories rather than guesses. However, confidence ratings alone do not establish that participants experienced a vivid false memory; confident errors can arise from response bias, familiarity, or metacognitive miscalibration. The operationalization therefore does not validly isolate the construct 'memory illusion' as claimed.
issues.quote: Therefore, isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.description: The task probes memory using a six-alternative recognition display that includes the mirrored counterpart on critical trials. This setup can induce source confusion or familiarity-driven selection from the test display itself, especially when participants are uncertain. The resulting errors need not reflect altered memory content. The authors acknowledge but dismiss this concern using asymmetry arguments that do not fully eliminate test-induced bias.
issues.quote:
The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed)...
...
Another cause of illusory reports could be confusion between the to-be-remembered target and the mirrored counterpart that is presented in the response screen.

issues.subcategory: feedback during main task may alter learning/expectations
issues.description: Participants received feedback during or after blocks in the main experiments. Because the study concerns expectation formation and memory bias, feedback can change strategies, confidence calibration, and learned priors across trials. This is especially problematic in experiments testing expectation-driven errors and in Experiment 2's manipulation of local expectations. No analysis examines practice/feedback effects over time.
issues.quote:
They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.
...
After each block the participant received feedback on her performance which included information about her average accuracy.

issues.subcategory: sequential Bayes stopping without adequate preregistration details
issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used Bayes-factor sequential stopping, but key details are missing: prior specification, exact testing schedule, whether optional stopping rules were fixed in advance, whether any interim peeking influenced design decisions, and whether all stopping analyses used the same exclusion rules as the final analyses. Without these details, the evidential interpretation is difficult to assess.
issues.quote:
Sample size was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test... Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.
...
once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.description: No preregistration is reported for hypotheses, exclusion rules, stopping rules, or analysis plans. Given the use of sequential Bayes stopping, post hoc collapsing over cue color, and multiple follow-up analyses, the absence of a preregistered plan limits confidence in confirmatory interpretation.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced ... Since this analysis showed no effects of cue colour ... the rest of the analysis was conducted while collapsing over the two cue colour conditions.

issues.description: In Experiment 2, cue color was first analyzed, then dropped and data were collapsed across it because no effect was found. This is a form of data-dependent analytic choice that can affect inferential calibration, especially without preregistration or full reporting of all models and robustness checks.
issues.quote: Since this analysis showed no effects of cue colour (see Results), the rest of the analysis was conducted while collapsing over the two cue colour conditions.

issues.subcategory: expectation manipulation confounded with color salience/luminance
issues.description: Experiment 2's cue-color manipulation uses red and blue stimuli with different reported luminance values, so any effect or null effect of the cue manipulation is confounded by perceptual differences in salience and discriminability. This compromises interpretation of the manipulation as purely expectation-based.
issues.quote: both the central fixation cross and the cue were either blue (CIE: 0.148, 0.078, luminance: 6.47 cd/m2) or red (CIE: 0.641, 0.341; luminance: 11.9 cd/m2).

issues.description: The transient expectation manipulation in Experiment 2 is not independently validated. Participants were unaware of the contingency by self-report, but no evidence is presented that the cue altered subjective expectation or criterion. A null effect therefore cannot distinguish absence of local expectation effects from failure of the manipulation.
issues.quote:
If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on 25% of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on 60% of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue.
...
The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.subcategory: mislabeling of ANOVA variables as independent variables in repeated-measures design
issues.description: The analyses are described as ANOVAs with repeated-measures factors listed as 'independent variables' and 'relative occurrence of high confidence selection' as the dependent variable. While not fatal, this description is conceptually sloppy and obscures whether participant-level repeated observations were properly modeled. More importantly, proportions bounded between 0 and 1 with many zeros are poorly matched to standard ANOVA assumptions.
issues.quote: error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type ..., memory delay ... and error type ... as independent variables and relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable.

issues.subcategory: use of ANOVA on sparse bounded proportions
issues.description: The dependent measures are cell-wise error proportions computed after substantial filtering to high-confidence trials, likely producing non-normal, heteroskedastic, and zero-inflated data. Repeated-measures ANOVA on such proportions is questionable; trial-level generalized mixed models would be more appropriate and would avoid listwise deletion from empty cells. The manuscript provides no diagnostics or justification for ANOVA suitability.
issues.quote:
The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA ...
...
Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.description: Experiment 3 explicitly uses listwise deletion because some participants had zero high-confidence responses in one or more cells. This method can bias results and reduce power, especially when missingness is not random but related to confidence and performance. No alternative handling or sensitivity analysis is reported.
issues.quote: Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.subcategory: missing trial-count justification for exclusion threshold
issues.description: The manuscript does not report expected numbers of critical high-confidence trials per cell for each experiment, making it hard to evaluate whether the >10 threshold is reasonable or whether some cells were inherently too sparse by design. This is particularly important because critical trials were only ~26% of all trials in Experiment 1.
issues.quote: Together, the critical trials made up ~220 trials, 26% of all trials in the experiment.

issues.description: The paper alternates between 0.75 s and 0.5 s as the short delay when summarizing findings. This inconsistency affects interpretation of which memory stage was tested and whether comparisons across experiments are validly described.
issues.quote:
In Experiment 1 ... the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset ...
...
Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)

issues.description: The General Discussion states Experiments 1 and 2 probed memory at 500 ms, but Experiment 1's short cue was 0.75 s and Experiment 2's short blank was 0.5 s followed by a cue, making the effective probe timing not directly equivalent. This misstates the design and overcompresses differences across experiments.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)

issues.description: Experiment 3 describes the variable-duration practice display with a parenthetical sentence that is grammatically broken and unclear, making the actual practice timing difficult to reconstruct. Replicability suffers because the exact sequence of practice durations is not fully clear.
issues.quote: Secondly, the display time for the memory display in practice trials was variable (where it was 2500 ms in for all practice trials in Experiment 2: In the first practice trials the memory display was presented for 1350 ms.

issues.subcategory: online data collection introduces uncontrolled stimulus conditions
issues.description: Experiment 4 was run online on participants' own laptops via Zoom/Neurotask, without reported control of screen size, viewing distance, refresh rate, timing accuracy, ambient lighting, or browser/device variability. Since the task depends on very brief 250 ms presentations and subtle mirror-orientation discrimination, lack of stimulus control threatens internal validity and comparability with lab-based experiments.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting ... which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.description: Across the lab experiments, critical display details are absent: monitor size/resolution/refresh rate, viewing distance, whether chinrest was used, and actual visual angle calibration procedure. These omissions hinder replication and assessment of whether 250 ms exposures were presented consistently.
issues.quote: The experiment was programmed in Matlab version 2012b using the Psychophysics Toolbox routines .

issues.description: The manuscript states conditions were 'randomly intermixed' but does not report whether randomization was constrained, whether target identities and mirrored counterparts were counterbalanced, or whether item-level effects were controlled. Given possible letter-specific asymmetries, item balancing is important.
issues.quote:
The three trial-types were randomly intermixed.
...
All conditions were randomly intermixed throughout the experiment.

issues.description: The interpretation hinges on 'world knowledge' about canonical letter orientation, but no direct measure of participants' familiarity, reading expertise, or item-specific prior strength is obtained. Thus the proposed construct is inferred rather than measured, and alternative explanations such as asymmetries in visual discriminability of specific mirrored pairs remain viable.
issues.quote: Instead ‘world knowledge’ (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.description: Different letters and their mirrored versions may vary markedly in perceptual confusability. The manuscript treats all real/pseudo-letter pairs as equivalent and provides no item analysis or control for pair-specific difficulty. Consequently, the pseudo-to-real asymmetry could partly reflect idiosyncratic item properties rather than generalized world-knowledge effects.
issues.quote:
Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment ...
...
Pseudo-letter targets were more likely than real-letter targets to evoke an expectation-induced illusory response

issues.description: The asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors is taken as evidence for world knowledge, but the design does not rule out alternative explanations such as greater perceptual fluency of canonical letters, differential verbal labeling ease, response preference for familiar symbols, or asymmetric encoding strength. These are related but not identical to the theoretical claim that top-down priors reshape memory content.
issues.quote: This suggests that world knowledge is a more important driver of illusory memories than visual similarity...

issues.description: The critique of fuzzy trace theory appears conceptually inaccurate. The manuscript states FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories and then says abundant false memories with high similarity are inconsistent with the data. That logic is reversed: abundant false memories in highly similar items would be consistent with such a prediction. The argument against FTT is therefore not valid as stated.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories . This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from letters to STM broadly
issues.description: The abstract and discussion generalize from mirrored-letter tasks to 'STM' and even 'perceptual representations' broadly. Yet all evidence comes from overlearned alphabetic stimuli in predominantly young university samples. Claims about short-term memory in general, or all perceptual representations, exceed the demonstrated scope.
issues.quote:
Together, these experiments show that expectations can reshape perceptual representations over short time scales...
...
Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions

issues.description: Samples were drawn largely from first-year psychology students at one university, with one online student sample. The manuscript does not adequately acknowledge that reading habits, alphabet expertise, age, and education could moderate the effect. Generalization to broader populations is uncertain.
issues.quote:
The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.
...
The participants participated for student credits within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.subcategory: claim that all stages of STM are susceptible not supported
issues.description: The General Discussion claims 'all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories,' yet later states the experiments do not test iconic memory and only suggest WM and fragile memory involvement. The broader statement is unsupported by the presented data.
issues.quote:
The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research...
...
Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM

issues.subcategory: conflation of working memory, fragile memory, and task manipulations
issues.description: The manuscript maps its cue/interference manipulations onto distinct memory stores (WM, FM) without direct process measures or accepted diagnostic criteria. These labels are treated as if the experiments isolate specific memory systems, but the tasks do not provide strong evidence for such stage-specific attribution.
issues.quote: Experiment 1 shows that when the memory cue is presented together with unrelated information, a trial-type most like a WM manipulation... Experiment 2-4 show that in a FM set-up illusory memories are also abundant.

issues.subcategory: absence of accuracy and confidence distributions
issues.description: The manuscript focuses on high-confidence error rates but does not provide complete descriptive statistics for overall accuracy, correct high-confidence responses, low-confidence responses, or confidence distributions by condition. Without these, it is difficult to evaluate metacognitive calibration, speed-accuracy tradeoffs, or whether changes in high-confidence error rates simply reflect shifts in confidence usage.
issues.quote: Included participants had on average 49.2% high confidence trial over all conditions ...

issues.description: No response time data are reported. RTs could help distinguish memory-based retrieval from strategic guessing or response biases and would aid interpretation of high-confidence errors. Their omission leaves an important gap in understanding the decision process.
issues.quote: After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options, and then indicated her confidence

issues.description: The manuscript's verbal labels for Bayes factors are nonstandard and asymmetric (e.g., BF < 0.33 called 'strong evidence for the null'; 0.33-1 'substantial evidence for the null'). While not fatal, this can overstate evidence against effects, especially with values near 0.33 or 1. More importantly, the prior settings underlying these BFs are not fully reported.
issues.quote: Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF < 0.33: strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33 - 1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis. 1 – 3: anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis...

issues.description: The Bayesian ANOVAs are reported without full prior details (e.g., default prior scales, whether JASP defaults were used unchanged, robustness checks). Because Bayes factors depend on prior specification, these omissions impede evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.subcategory: training task may select for atypical visual-memory abilities
issues.description: Experiment 1 required participants to pass a separate cued change detection training task before taking part. This selects for individuals with better performance or motivation in visual memory tasks, potentially biasing the sample and reducing comparability with later experiments that lacked this gatekeeping procedure.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct ... We adopted this procedure to ensure that all participants were motivated, and possessed a minimal proficiency at visual memory tasks.

issues.description: The four experiments differ in sample source, task environment (lab vs online), target frequencies, response display composition, delays, and practice procedures. Yet the discussion presents them as converging cleanly on the same phenomenon without sufficiently considering how procedural changes may alter the effect or limit direct comparability.
issues.quote:
In 4 experiments we thus test 3 hypotheses...
...
Four experiments consistently show that illusory memories can arise

issues.description: The manuscript treats the irrelevant second display as increasing memory decay through interference, but the manipulation may also alter attention, expectancy, masking, or confusion at test. Therefore stronger illusions in interference conditions cannot be attributed specifically to STM trace deterioration.
issues.quote: To increase memory decay through task-irrelevant interference, a second display was included in each trial. This display consisted of randomly selected letters, unrelated to the memory display. Participants were instructed to ignore this second display.

issues.subcategory: contradiction in Experiment 4 delay effect description
issues.description: The text says there was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays for mirrored targets (5%) than for real targets (4%). But 5% is larger, not smaller. This error creates confusion about the pattern underlying the non-significant three-way interaction.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.subcategory: missing exact cell counts after exclusions
issues.description: The manuscript reports percentages but not the exact numbers of trials contributing to each condition after exclusions and high-confidence filtering. Given sparse critical cells and participant exclusions, exact denominators are needed to assess stability of the percentages.
issues.quote: Figure 4 shows the memory illusions and other error rates for high confidence trials... Participants were more likely to select the mirrored (pseudo) counterpart of a target than to commit other types of errors (18% vs 11%...)
